cards.example: Natural reply: «Muy bien, gracias, ¿y a ti?» — warmer and more natural than textbook «¿cómo estás?».

cards.front: Me pones un café con leche, por favor.
cards.hint: meh POH-nehs oon kah-FEH kohn LEH-cheh
cards.back: Could I get a coffee with milk, please?
cards.example: In Spain & Latin America, «¿Me pones…?» or «Me regala…?» sounds native; avoid literal «Puedo tener».

cards.hint: PWEH-dehs ah-BLAR oon POH-koh mahs dehs-PAH-syoh
cards.back: Can you speak a little more slowly?
cards.example: Pair with a smile and «Todavía estoy aprendiendo» (I'm still learning) to unlock instant patience.

cards.front: Ser vs. Estar: «Soy listo» vs. «Estoy listo»
cards.back: Soy listo = I am clever · Estoy listo = I am ready
cards.example: Memory hook: SER is essence/identity; ESTAR is state/location («How you feel and where you are, always use the verb estar»).

cards.front: Mucho gusto, me llamo… ¿De dónde eres?
cards.back: Nice to meet you, my name is… Where are you from?
cards.example: Answer with «Soy de… pero vivo en…» (I'm from… but I live in…).

cards.front: Disculpa, ¿queda lejos la estación de metro?
cards.back: Excuse me, is the metro station far from here?
cards.example: Reply cue: «A cinco minutos andando, todo recto» = 5 minutes walking, straight ahead.

cards.back: What do you recommend I try here?
cards.example: Follow up at the end: «La cuenta, cuando puedas» (The check, whenever you can).

cards.back: Do you feel like grabbing a drink/bite this afternoon?
cards.example: Reply: «¡Claro, me encantaría! ¿A qué hora quedamos?» (Sure, I'd love to! What time shall we meet?).

cards.front: ¿Se puede pagar con tarjeta o solo en efectivo?
cards.back: Can I pay by card, or cash only?
cards.example: «Se puede + infinitive» is a superpower structure meaning 'Is it possible to…?'.

cards.back: I have been studying Spanish for two weeks.
cards.example: Example: «Llevo tres años viviendo aquí» = I've been living here for three years.

cards.front: Tengo ganas de viajar este verano.
cards.back: I really feel like / am looking forward to traveling this summer.
cards.example: Short version: «¡Qué ganas!» = I can't wait!

cards.back: It depends · Actually / in fact · By the way
cards.example: Connectors buy your brain 2 calm seconds to assemble the next sentence naturally.

cards.front: Suelo despertarme a las siete y caminar.
cards.back: I usually wake up at seven and take a walk.
cards.example: Instead of repeating «usualmente», natives use «suelo + verb»: «Suelo leer antes de dormir».

cards.front: Se me olvidó la llave · No pasa nada.
cards.back: I accidentally forgot the key · No worries at all.
cards.example: Also works for «Se me cayó» (I dropped it) and «Se me hizo tarde» (I ended up running late).

cards.front: Ayer fui al mercado y encontré fruta increíble.
cards.back: Yesterday I went to the market and found incredible fruit.
cards.example: Note: «fui» is the past tense of both «ir» (to go) and «ser» (to be); context always makes it clear.

cards.front: Mañana voy a practicar quince minutos más.
cards.back: Tomorrow I'm going to practice fifteen more minutes.
cards.example: Works for 90% of future situations before you ever need formal future conjugations.

cards.front: Espero que tengas un buen día.
cards.hint: Esperar que triggers present subjunctive (tener → tengas)
cards.back: I hope you have a great day.
cards.example: Same pattern: «Ojalá que haga buen tiempo» (Hopefully the weather is nice).

cards.front: Poco a poco se llega lejos.
cards.hint: Literal: Little by little one arrives far
cards.back: Step by step, you go far — consistency beats intensity.
cards.example: The MindLoop philosophy in six Spanish words.
